info.text: Four familiar strands of television history, followed by questions about the innovations hiding behind the programmes.

citations.title: A Brief History of the Teleprompter
citations.author: Jimmy Stamp

clusters.name: Situation Comedy
clusters.fact: The television sitcom repeatedly reinvents a durable setup: recurring characters negotiating family, friendship, and work within a familiar place.

clusters.name: Science Fiction
clusters.fact: Television science fiction turns speculative ideas into continuing worlds, giving audiences time to live with their social and technological consequences.

clusters.name: Crime & Mystery
clusters.fact: Crime television ranges from self-contained puzzles to serialized portraits of institutions, investigators, victims, and offenders.

clusters.name: Animation
clusters.fact: Television animation grew from economical limited-animation production into a medium for family comedy, superhero drama, satire, and serialized fantasy.

lenses.prompt: The producer of which series patented an in-camera teleprompter that let performers read while looking toward the audience?
lenses.explanation: Jess Oppenheimer, producer of I Love Lucy, patented an in-camera teleprompter that projected text in front of the lens, allowing performers to appear to look directly toward viewers.

lenses.prompt: Which mystery series usually shows the crime and culprit first, turning 'Who did it?' into 'How will the detective prove it?'
lenses.explanation: Columbo made the inverted detective story its signature. The audience watches the murder and cover-up, then follows Lieutenant Columbo as he finds the discrepancy that exposes the culprit.

lenses.prompt: Which programme was the first animated situation comedy made for American prime-time television?
lenses.explanation: The Flintstones premiered on ABC in 1960 as the first animated situation comedy produced for prime time, demonstrating that television animation could attract a broad evening audience.
